entries.title: Shuttle: the launch line carries the first turn
entries.brief: /color already goes through the verified send; the skill-load message or the prompt should ride the launch line so only later turns are typed
entries.body:
## Why

Shuttle types `/color <color>` into a fresh session's pane, and with skills it types the skill-load message and then the prompt as well.
Every typed send is a chance for a lost or half-landed message, and the operator finds the typing clumsy (2026-10-08).

## Facts (Claude Code 2.1.294 CLI reference)

- No CLI flag, settings key or environment variable sets the session color; `/color` in the session is the only way.
- The positional `claude "<text>"` submits its text as the first user turn of an interactive session, and a slash command or skill invocation works there.
- Only one positional prompt exists, so the launch line carries one first turn.

## Proposal

- The launch line carries the first turn in every case: the skill-load message when skills are named, else the prompt, so only the turns after the first are typed.
- `/color` stays typed, as there is no launch-time alternative, but goes through shuttle's verified send once `shuttle-send` lands, after the session is ready.

## Priority

Operator, 2026-10-08: low; the typed skill load is robust, and the launch line saves only a little time.

## Done on 2026-10-08

`/color` goes through shuttle's verified send after the session is ready (main e12fb6afb, with the settle wait from 7b3d140cb).
What remains is the first proposal bullet: the launch line carries the first turn.

entries.title: lyx pause: stop every run at once, safely and on purpose
entries.brief: A hub-wide pause that interrupts every Claude session with Esc within seconds, unlike the step-boundary pauses, recorded as ordered so no failure or idle path fires
entries.body:
## Why

The operator suspends the laptop while runs are in flight.
A sleep can cut a network call or an agent turn midway (a weft push hung a batten run for 2.5 hours after a hibernate, #458), and after resume idle notices fire for time that was only sleep.

The existing `lyx batten pause` and `lyx loom pause` only set a request the machine consumes at its next producer boundary: they kill nothing, so an agent turn, a Webster batch or a review round runs on until it ends, which can be an hour.
That is not enough to make the hub safe to suspend.

## Proposal (operator, 2026-10-08)

- One hub-wide verb, named `lyx pause` (the operator's choice of name), that safely stops every lyx process within a short time.
- It gives running work a few seconds to finish cleanly, such as a bash command completing.
- It interrupts every running Claude Code instance by sending Esc.
- A pause is ordered and intentional: it must not trigger the paths for an unexpected stop, such as batten notices, the agents-idle or driver-dead conditions, review-round failures or crash recovery.
- The step-boundary pause is not good enough and goes: it is how Millhouse had to pause, and lyx now has the means to interrupt agents directly (shuttle's session state from hooks, the reed panes, shuttle's stop verb).

## Open design points

- Resuming: whether a matching verb resumes every paused run where it stood, and how each role takes up its interrupted turn (loom's `interrupt_policy` already distinguishes `reinvoke` from `handback`).
- Scope: whether the orch session is paused too, or only runs.
- Per-run use: whether `lyx pause <slug>` pauses one run the same way, now that the boundary pause goes.
- Relation to shuttle's stop verb from `shuttle-send`, which settles a run's record before removing its strand.

entries.title: reed: strands state their size; parallel agents share the window evenly
entries.brief: Replace the one collapse-all-but-the-newest rule with per-strand sizing: content-sized panes like the runs overview, and parallel agents that share space evenly
entries.body:
## Why

reed has one layout rule (`internal/reedengine/doc.go`, "The layout rule"): the strands stack in insertion order, every strand but the bottom-most takes `collapsed_rows` rows, and the bottom-most takes every remaining row.
It fits a run whose newest agent is the one that matters, and nothing else:

- `runs-overview` wants a small pane under the orch, sized to its content, with the orch above keeping the space; today the orch would collapse to `collapsed_rows` and the overview would grow.
- `multi-agent-producer` runs N agents in parallel, none more important than the others; each needs a large share of the window, and none may collapse.

## Proposal (operator, 2026-10-08)

- A strand states how it is sized instead of taking its size from its position.
- At least two kinds: a fixed or content-sized strand (the overview: as few rows as show all its lines), and a sharing strand that splits the remaining space evenly with the other sharing strands.
- The agents of one multi-agent step share the window evenly, side by side or stacked; which of the two is open.
- The collapsed stack of finished agents may stay as one kind among these, for strands kept only for reference.

## Columns (operator, 2026-10-08)

The layout rules need a broader revision: tmux under reed can show any arrangement, so stacking strands side by side in columns, rather than in rows, is tempting as the main rule.

## Open

- Side by side (columns) or stacked rows for parallel agents, or a rule by window width.
- Who sets a strand's kind: the spawning producer through its seat table (`multi-agent-producer`), or reed by role.
- How `runs-overview`'s content-sized pane learns its height as runs come and go, and whether reed re-applies the layout on each change.

entries.title: Spawn audit log: every process lyx starts is recorded and traceable
entries.brief: One recorded launch path and a hub-wide spawn log with owner, argv and resource use, plus a sampler and a summary verb, so a process storm can be traced after a crash
entries.body:
## Seen

On 2026-10-08 the operator's machine froze and needed a hard reset at about 20:12 CEST while four runs were in flight.
`sar` shows about 800 process starts per second between 19:50 and 20:00, about 500 more live processes by 20:10,
and the user slice at its 16 GiB `MemoryHigh` with swap full, so reclaim thrashed (8366 major faults/s, 768 MB/s reads).
Only about 15 claude sessions and 9 subagents started in that window, and nothing in lyx's logs says what else started the processes or which run, strand or command owned them.
The operator has seen an earlier storm of 100+ claude panes in reed, and could not trace that one either.

## Idea

Every process lyx starts goes through one recorded launch path that appends an audit line to a hub-wide spawn log:
time, pid, parent pid, the lyx command and trace id that started it, hub, run slug, strand name, executable and argv,
and on exit the duration, exit status, peak RSS and bytes read and written (from `rusage` and `/proc/<pid>/io`).
This covers tmux servers, sessions and panes, claude launches, git, and `go build`/`go test` in verify gates.
A sampler, such as the reed watchdog, also records per-strand process-tree counts and memory every few seconds,
so the state just before a freeze survives a reboot.
`lyx` gains a read verb that summarises the log by minute, run, strand and executable, so a storm can be traced to its source after the fact.

entries.title: Config-driven file log level
entries.brief: logger.yaml gains a level key for the file trace, independent of -v, so a crash can be traced without a rebuild
entries.body:
## Seen

The trace files written for each lyx invocation hold only high-level messages, and `_lyx/config/logger.yaml` sets only retention (`trace_retention_count`, `trace_retention_days`).
The file log has no configurable level, so after the 2026-10-08 crash the traces could not show what lyx's subcommands did.
Activity-ranked pruning also left the per-minute invocation counts incomplete.

## Idea

`logger.yaml` gains a `level` key (error, warn, info, debug) for the file trace, independent of the `-v` console verbosity, with info as the default.
Every engine logs its decisions and external calls at info or debug, so raising the level makes most of what lyx does traceable without a rebuild.
The spawn audit stays always on, whatever the level, because it cannot be turned on after a crash.

entries.title: Haiku 5.5 for the Bouncer judge: is its ruling simple enough
entries.brief: The driver already runs on Haiku 5.5; decide per Bouncer row whether the judge ruling is simple enough for Haiku, trial it, and switch only where it holds
entries.body:
## Seen

The operator benchmarked Haiku 5.5 on 2026-10-08 (`docs/benchmarks/haiku-5-5.md`): on one fully specified coding task it scored as well as Sonnet and Opus at medium, at a fraction of the cost, but took about twice as long and grew its context to 74–132k.
The driver steps one run through `lyx shed step` and answers its waits, and the judge rules on a fixed question per round; neither writes code or long prose.

## Driver switched (operator, 2026-10-08)

`driver` is `haiku[medium]` in `loom.yaml` from 2026-10-08, for runs started after that.
Compare the driver row of the token report per role, and the hub interventions, against the Sonnet runs before it.

## What the task decides: the judge (operator, 2026-10-10)

Switching the judge is one config key; the task's work is deciding whether it is sound.
The question is whether the judge's job is simple enough for Haiku 5.5: read what each Bouncer row's judge and seed passes receive and must rule on, and judge where a wrong verdict lets a defect through or sends good work back.

- Read the judge stencils and a sample of past verdicts from the usage and review records, and name the rows, if any, whose ruling needs more than Haiku holds.
- Trial the judge on Haiku on one run and compare against Sonnet runs: verdicts later overturned, extra review rounds, hub interventions and token cost.
- Switch only the rows where both the reading and the trial hold; the other roles stay as they are.

## Seen in use

- 2026-10-10, `bolt-and-store`: the Haiku 5.5 driver read its prompt, summarized its rules, and ended the turn asking "Tell me when to start", although the prompt says it runs autonomously with no operator to ask.
  The Haiku drivers of `multi-llm-producer` and `daemon-wakeups`, on the same prompt, started stepping at once; a message from the orch got it going.
  Fixed in 189fd59c8: the driver stencil now says the prompt is the go-ahead and a turn never ends on a question.

## Analysis and decision (operator, 2026-10-10)

The analysis is in `docs/research/haiku-judge.md` (5459376bb): keep Sonnet on the Discussion-Bouncer judge; trial Haiku 5.5 on the Plan-Bouncer and Webster-Bouncer judges; seed passes are safe for Haiku.
The `judge` key sets all three rows at once, so the judge stays on Sonnet for now.
The trial waits for the note `per-role-models`, which gives each row's judge its own model key, and then runs Haiku 5.5 on the Plan-Bouncer and Webster-Bouncer judges only.

## Decided: the judge stays on Sonnet (operator, 2026-10-11)

The analysis showed nothing to gain: the token report per role over six runs (2026-10-10) puts the judge at 2.8% and seed at 1.1% of run weight, against 32% for Burler review and fix and 24% for Webster with its forks.
The judge stays on Sonnet and no Haiku judge trial runs; token savings go to Burler and Webster instead.
`per-role-models` is still wanted on its own merits.

entries.title: Burler runs its round on MultiLLMProducer
entries.brief: The fixer becomes the chair and the reviewer advisor-1 in one seat table, replacing roundHalves and await-review
entries.body:
## Goal

Burler's review round runs on `MultiLLMProducer` instead of its own two-agent wiring (operator, 2026-10-08).

## Today

Burler's round has run two agents ad hoc since 572ab84e8: `roundHalves` in `internal/burlerengine/engine.go` starts the reviewer and the fixer, and the fixer waits on the review through `lyx burler await-review`.
The round wires six stencils (two orchestrator templates, three step files, a focus directive) plus per-segment rubrics through Go code spread over several packages.

## Wanted

- The fixer is the `chair` and the reviewer `advisor-1`, declared in one seat table.
- The ad hoc wiring (`roundHalves`, `await-review`) goes; the round's outcome, review files and Bouncer contract stay as they are.
- Fanned rounds (`discussion_fan`, `plan_fan`) keep working; whether a fan's lenses become advisor seats or stay forks of the reviewer is decided in Discussion.

## Required (operator, 2026-10-11)

- **Warm cache.** Today the fixer waits through `lyx burler await-review`, capped under the 5-minute prompt-cache lifetime so every re-run keeps its cache warm (`internal/burlercli/await.go:25`).
  A seats chair instead ends its turn and waits idle, so a review longer than 5 minutes would wake the fixer on a cold cache every round.
  The chair keeps its cache warm at least as well as today, using the general capped wait command that `twill-discusser` builds, not a Burler-specific one.
- **No false stall notices.** Folded in from `seats-chair-wait-notice` below: with the fixer as chair, every Burler round of every run would otherwise send the parent stall notices.

## Seats chair waits reach the parent as stall notices (was `seats-chair-wait-notice`)

### Seen (2026-10-11, discussion bench)

Every time a seats chair ends its turn to wait, for an advisor's up line or for an advisor's answers, shuttle sends the parent a "turn end held, output files missing" notice (`internal/shuttleengine/hold.go:53`, `notifyHeld`).
These waits are planned by the chair stencil, so the notices are false stall alarms; each advisor run in the bench sent the orch three to four of them.
Advisors are quiet because `internal/seatengine/prompt.go:160` sets `QuietHold: !isChair`; the chair is not.
Answering a notice wakes the chair for a turn, which sends another notice.

### Idea

Suppress the held notice for a chair while any advisor has an unanswered batch or has not yet sent its up line, and keep it for a chair that ends a turn with no advisor work outstanding, which is a real stall.

entries.title: Plan-Write on MultiLLMProducer: advisors gather facts and check cards
entries.brief: Later: Plan-Write as the chair, with an advisor that maps callers, tests and verify commands per package, and possibly one that checks each card as it is written
entries.body:
## Seen

Plan gate rejects and Plan-Review rounds come mostly from facts the planner got wrong or missed: an uncovered caller, a verify line in the wrong module, a nested fixture module, a card over its test budget.
Plan is one document that must hang together, so two agents writing it at once would conflict.

## Idea

Plan-Write runs on `MultiLLMProducer` (task `multi-llm-producer`), the planner as the `chair`, with advisors doing work the chair would otherwise do itself:

1. A code-reading advisor maps, for each package the plan touches, its callers, tests, nested modules and verify commands, and answers the chair's questions from that map.
2. A card-checking advisor reads each card as the chair finishes it and checks its scope, `Edit:` list, verify lines and test budget, so the chair fixes it while its context is fresh rather than in a later review round.

A third shape, advisors writing the cards of their own batch from the chair's overview, is faster on large tasks but makes the cards hard to keep consistent; left out unless the first two fall short.

## When

Operator, 2026-10-08: later, after `discussion-multi-llm`.
Plan runs on `fable[high]` as a single agent from 2026-10-08; this is the next step if that does not reduce plan gate rejects and Plan-Review rounds.

entries.title: One owner for child-process lifetime in internal/proc
entries.brief: Fold lyx gate test's process-group, Pdeathsig and job-object setup into internal/proc beside ConfigureGroupKill
entries.body:
Two process-lifetime implementations exist once `gate-test-scope` and `git-robustness` both land: `internal/proc` `ConfigureGroupKill` (process group, group SIGKILL on cancel, shared by `verifyrun` and `gitexec`) and `lyx gate test`'s own child lifetime (process group, group kill on a caught signal, Linux `Pdeathsig`, Windows kill-on-close job object).
The orch kept them apart on 2026-10-10 so the two parallel branches would merge without conflict.

Idea: move the `lyx gate` child-lifetime setup into `internal/proc` beside `ConfigureGroupKill`, so one package owns child-process lifetime, and consider whether `verifyrun` and `gitexec` should gain the parent-death signal and job object as well.

The package also lacks a `doc.go`; its file headers carry the description (PR-Gate review of PR #483).

entries.title: Bench the chair-and-advisors Discussion against the solo writer before switching it on
entries.brief: Same tasks through both producers, compare review rounds, findings, tokens and time; the operator watches a live run before it goes on
entries.body:
## Seen

`discussion-multi-llm` adds a second Discussion producer: a chair that writes, with advisors that study the code and answer its design questions live.
The default keeps the existing solo Discussion-Write, so landing it changes no run.

## Idea

Before any hub selects the chair-and-advisors producer, bench it against the solo writer on the same tasks: Discussion-Review rounds and findings, parent-review outcome, token cost per seat, and wall time.
Then the operator watches it in action on at least one live run before it is switched on.

## Operator decisions (2026-10-10)

- Models for the trial: the chair on `opus[medium]`, one advisor on `sonnet[high]`.
- Not in production until the bench and a watched run have shown it holds.

## Retiring the single producer (operator, 2026-10-10)

The seats producer with an empty `discussion_advisors` list covers the single writer's job: one chair prompt for every advisor count says "use your advisors if you have any; with none, decide each question yourself as you judge best", with no conditional rendering.
Once that is tested, the single producer is parked, since seats with N=0 covers it; the bench should include an N=0 run against solo to show they match.

## Bench design (operator, 2026-10-11)

Runs after `seats-chair-first` has landed and is deployed, so the chair starts first and asks in rounds.
A fresh agent run from the prime drives it; neither loom nor darn fits, since the output is a report, not a change.

- Reference: `webster-stability`, whose Discussion solo `fable[high]` wrote on base 800a0e892.
  Its first draft (records repo, `archive/webster-stability/*`, commit 82e8b0f9), its final discussion after three Discussion-Review rounds (e77a1372), and each round's findings are the answer key; `loop-small-bugs` (base 292bec755) is the fallback.
- Configurations, at most one advisor:
  - seats (chair, advisor): (`opus[high]`, `opus[medium]`), (`opus[high]`, `sonnet[high]`), (`opus[high]`, `sonnet[medium]`), (`opus[medium]`, `sonnet[medium]`);
  - seats with N=0: `fable[medium]`, `opus[high]`, `opus[medium]`;
  - control: the single producer on `opus[medium]`, against seats N=0 on `opus[medium]`.
- Method: one bench pair per configuration, reset to the base, models in the pair's own `loom.yaml` (`discussion_producer`, `discussion`, `discussion_advisors`), `lyx loom step` through Discussion-Write only, then the decision record and support log copied out.
- Order: one DualDW run first, (`opus[high]`, `sonnet[high]`), which the operator watches; the rest run in parallel once that one holds.
- Grading: each reference finding the Bouncer kept, avoided or repeated; decision overlap with the final discussion, new and missing decisions; writer tokens and wall time (`tools/tokencount`); how many batches the chair sent and whether it used the answers.
- Report: `docs/research/discussion-bench.md`.
- Second round (operator, 2026-10-11): a separate bench round with two advisors, such as chair `opus[high]` with advisors `opus[medium]` and `sonnet[high]`, testing whether a broader first draft beats a later Burler review-and-fix round in strength and speed.
  It should also measure how many Burler rounds each draft needs to converge and the total time and tokens to the final discussion, not only the draft against the answer key.
  A co-chair variant (see `discussion-advisor-mode`) is a candidate for the same comparison.
- The operator confirmed (2026-10-11) that the bench agent may create and tear down the bench pairs, add a temporary board note per bench slug holding a copy of the reference task body (the writer reads it with `lyx board get`) and remove them after, and approve each bench pair's Discussion parent-review gate itself.

## Seen in the first run (2026-10-11)

The operator, watching `dbench-ohsh`, saw that the chair-advisor back and forth takes time and remarked that each batch should carry many questions.
The first round runs on the current chair stencil, unchanged, to learn whether the advisor setup is worth having; if it is, a candidate change is for the chair to send every question it has in batch 1 and only follow-ups after.

entries.title: Discussion advisors: operator-named areas per advisor on top of the landed all-advisors default
entries.brief: Each discussion_advisors entry takes an optional area (a lens, as in review fans); without one the advisor answers every question
entries.body:
## Seen

The chair-and-advisors Discussion (`discussion-multi-llm`) sends every question batch to every advisor, by the operator's PR-Gate ruling on PR #504 (2026-10-10).
The first draft instead gave each advisor its own area of the design, which narrows each advisor's view but spreads the study.

## Idea

Support both, selected per hub in `loom.yaml` (for example `discussion_advisor_mode: all | areas`, default `all`), with the value passed to the chair stencil as a marker.
Decide after `discussion-multi-llm-bench`, which can compare the two modes on the same tasks.

## Operator-named areas

The operator also wants to choose which area each advisor studies (2026-10-10), rather than leaving the split to the chair.
One shape: each `discussion_advisors` entry carries a model-spec plus an optional area, for example `{model: sonnet[high], area: error-handling}`, and the area names a lens text the advisor stencil includes, the way Burler's review fans name lenses (`correctness`, `error-handling`, `test-gaps`).
An entry without an area answers every question; an entry with one still sees every batch but answers from its lens.
This could replace the `all | areas` switch: the per-entry area is the selection.

## Co-chair (operator, 2026-10-11)

An alternative to an advisor: one seat is a co-chair that does its own exploration of the code and the task rather than only answering the chair's batches, so the draft gets a second independent study.
How the co-chair's findings reach the chair, and who writes the decision record, is open.

## Lens advisors as forks of the chair (2026-10-11)

The operator compares lens advisors with Burler's review fan, whose lens forks each review from one focus.
Burler's lenses are forks of the reviewer: they inherit its context and cached prefix and run on its model.
Seats advisors are fresh sessions on their own models, and each re-reads the code; in the first bench run (`dbench-ohsh`) the advisor's cache reads exceeded the chair's.
A variant: fork the lens advisors from the chair once it has read the task and code, so each lens starts with the chair's study at little cost, at the price of running on the chair's model.
Fresh-session advisors give breadth through different models, chair forks through different focus; a later bench can compare the two.
Lenses need a producer change either way: today the engine and chair stencil send every batch to every advisor with no focus.

## Board advisor in place of parent review (2026-10-11)

The operator asks whether an advisor with a board lens could take over Discussion's parent review, whose job is mostly checking the draft against everything else planned on the board.
Parent review also checks the draft against operator decisions made in the orch chat but not yet on the board, and against runs in flight; the one parent-review reject on 2026-10-11 (`per-role-models` round 1, seed model) was of that kind, which no advisor could have caught.
Proposal: put a board-lens advisor in the second bench round and compare what it catches with what parent review catches before making parent review optional.

## Advisor answers (operator, 2026-10-11)

Advisors write too much.
When an advisor agrees with the chair's pick, it says so in one line with no reasoning, since "I agree because ..." is clutter for the chair.
Every extension, correction or departure is explained.

## When (operator, 2026-10-11)

Advisors with different roles is a later enhancement.
The first DualDW bench runs one advisor at most, answering every batch as a plain assistant.

entries.title: Lens fan: master pre-reads the cited code before forking, forks get a read budget
entries.brief: Make the lens fan work as designed: the master reads the cited code (and judges nothing) before forking, each fork has a tool-call budget, and Discussion and Plan use their own fans
entries.body:
## Seen

The lens fan's design: the master reviewer reads most of what the round needs first, then forks, so each lens fork inherits that reading through the cache and needs little new reading, which keeps a fork cheap enough for a Sonnet medium reviewer.
The first fanned run (`webster-replan-state`, Discussion rounds 1-4 and Plan round 1) did not work that way; the analysis is in `docs/research/lens-fan-cost-analysis.md`:

- The master forked after reading only the target, instructions and stencil (39-74k context), no code, then told every fork to verify the Decisions' premises against the code.
  In Discussion round 1 the master read 19 code files first, and its forks took 32 turns and 152k fresh tokens; rounds 2-4 took 81-125 fork turns and 435-485k fresh.
- Inheritance through the cache works; cost scales with fork turns, about 3.5-4k fresh tokens per turn.
  32-46% of fork file reads duplicated another fork's.
- Fanned Discussion rounds cost 301-638k fresh against 86-121k for solo Opus rounds; Plan round 1 cost 901k fanned against 202-227k solo.
  The fan raised more MEDIUM and LOW findings, not more BLOCKING ones, and about half of raw fork findings were duplicates across lenses.

The responsible text is `clusterRulesBlock` in `internal/burlerengine/prompt.go`: "After exploring the target fully" never says to read the code the target cites, and "Fetch only what your lens needs" sets no budget.
The `standard` fan also points code lenses at design documents.

## Idea

Revise the fan so it works as designed:

- the master is told every lens of the fan up front, and before it spawns any fork it explores, for each lens, what that lens will need and reads it, so the forks inherit one shared reading instead of each exploring on its own (lyx cannot pick the relevant code itself: Discussion review is exploratory, so the master's judgment chooses what to read);
- the master judges nothing before the fork point: a review written before forking would colour every fork, so the master's own holistic review stays after the forks are spawned;
- each fork is told its context already holds the code, and gets a tool-call budget (about 6) for reading only what is missing; forks spending their budget show in the usage record that the master read too little;
- Discussion-Review and Plan-Review use the `discussion` and `plan` fans instead of `standard`.

Estimate: about 200-250k fresh tokens per round, about 2x a solo Opus round instead of 5-6x.

## Operator decisions (2026-10-10)

- The fan stays off in the hub until this task lands and a fanned run shows the estimate holds.
- Until then Discussion-Review and Plan-Review run solo on `opus[medium]`, and Webster-Review on `sonnet[medium]`.

## Research (fan-lab, 2026-10-10)

A research agent replayed `webster-replan-state` Discussion round 2 standalone (`lyx burler run`) per variant, master and forks `sonnet[medium]`; the full reports are `docs/research/lens-fan-lab-phase0.md` and `lens-fan-lab-phase1.md`.
Variants: A today's text; B a lens-agnostic reading checklist in step 1; C B plus a 6-call fork budget; D C plus a reading manifest the master writes before spawning.

| Run | Fan | Master code pre-reads | Fork tool calls | Review side fresh | Verdict | F1 (BLOCKING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | discussion | 0 | 2 | 216k | APPROVED | no |
| B | discussion | 2 | 8 | 154k | APPROVED | no |
| C | discussion | 2 | 0 | 133k | APPROVED | no |
| D | discussion | 12 | 1 | 198k | APPROVED | no |
| D | standard | 3 | 1 | 154k | APPROVED | no |
| original round 2 | standard, sonnet[high] | 0 | 135 | 619k | BLOCKING | yes |

Findings:

- Only the manifest (D) makes a Sonnet-medium master pre-read; in A-C it read instruction 2 at once and forked after the board entry and a few pattern files.
- No master judged anything before the spawn, in any variant.
- Only the D runs reproduced round 2's code-grounded MEDIUMs; A-C findings were text-level.
- No run found F1, which needs one hop past the target's citations (the D7 guard on `push` → `Fabric.Commit` → `SpawnDetachedPush`); at medium effort the forks barely read in any variant, so no one made the hop.
- Fork cost is driven by effort, not the budget: the original's 485k fork fresh came from `sonnet[high]` forks told to verify against code.
- A D round costs about 150-200k review side, still 1.5-2x a solo `opus[medium]` round.
- Every fork already inherits instruction 2 and so every lens, since the master reads it before spawning.

Recommendation: adopt D, with a checklist line for callers and spawned processes (untested). Step 1 (`clusterPrereadBlock`, explore file only, cluster rounds only):

```
## Reading for the fork reviewers

This round fans out: in step 2 you spawn fork reviewers, and each fork inherits your context as it stands at the spawn.
Your reading in this step is the forks' reading, so read here what the review will need, once, instead of leaving each fork to read it again.

Before you leave this step, read:

- every file the target names, at the definitions of the symbols it cites;
- for each symbol the target changes, guards or removes: its direct callers and callees, and every path that reaches it from another process, such as a child the code spawns or a command that calls the guarded verb in-process;
- the `pattern/` background file of every PATTERN entry the target names or touches;
- the board entry of the task the target belongs to, through `lyx board get`;
- the failure, restart and resume paths of each change the target makes.

Read definitions and call sites, not whole files: a fork re-reads its inherited context on every turn.
Judge nothing while you read: write no finding, verdict or assessment, not even in a status line or a note to yourself.
A judgement in your context before the spawn colours every fork; your own review starts after the forks are spawned.

End this step with a reading manifest as a plain message: one line per file and symbol you read, grouped by the part of the target it serves.
The manifest names what you read and nothing about what you found.
```

Step 2 (`clusterRulesBlock`), replacing the spawn trigger, the fork boilerplate and the holistic paragraph; the consolidation paragraph is unchanged:

```
This is a cluster round: as soon as step 1's reading is done, spawn ALL of the fork reviewers below in a SINGLE message via the Agent tool with `subagent_type: "fork"`, one per lens listed here — never pass a `name` (named forks silently lose inherited context).

Lenses for this round:

<lenses>

Each fork's prompt is this boilerplate plus that lens's emphasis text, and nothing else: never add a direction to verify against the code or to read files.
Your inherited context already holds the target, the rules and the code the target rests on; review from it.
The reading manifest in your context lists what is already read; check it before any tool call.
You may make at most 6 tool calls, each only for something your lens needs that the manifest lacks, such as a caller or a spawned process one hop beyond it, and never to re-read what your context already shows.
End your final message with one line per tool call you made: what you read and why your context lacked it.
You are READ-ONLY — never Write/Edit/delete any file, never run any git command, never touch the two round output files, and never call the Agent tool yourself (forks cannot nest); return your findings ONLY as your final message, each with a severity, a class, a location, and a one-line summary.

While the forks run, YOU (the handler) do your own HOLISTIC review — architecture, cross-file invariants, PATTERN-fit — from the same context, reading further only where it or a fork's read list shows a gap, and prepare the ground truths and the severity rubric you will judge every finding against.
```

## Confirming run (2026-10-10): parked

The recommended text on the standard fan at `sonnet[high]` aborted at the 300k cap with no review written: review side 354k, $3.19, 288 s active.
Three forks raised F1 through their hop budget, so the pre-read and the hop line work at high effort, but the round is slower than solo `opus[medium]` (225 s, $1.45, found F1) and about twice the price.
Solo `opus[medium]` stays the reviewer; this entry is parked as a note.
Two hand-built packs were then tried on solo `opus[medium]`, one run each:

- A body dump (the bodies of the 35 symbols the target cites, about 20k tokens, in a file read first): 312 s, $1.93 review side, missed the BLOCKING finding.
- A kick-start pack in quarry's `RenderKickstartPack` format (a glyph→span line and a signature line per glyph, 35 glyphs, 5.3 KB), injected into the first prompt with "read all listed spans in parallel, in one turn, before doing anything else": 316 s, $1.94 review side, found the BLOCKING finding (1 BLOCKING / 4 MEDIUM).

The operator doubts the second run applied the kick-start as designed either, and will look at it later.
Plain solo stays faster and cheaper for review on this fixture; the kick-start pack's measured case remains the implementer and the Burler fixer (`kick-start-pack`).

Open if the fan comes back:

- The landing text must say "go straight on to step 2 in the same turn": the master ended its turn after posting the manifest.
- The `discussion` fan has no lens aimed at a guard's callers; `scenarios` is the natural owner if a lens change is wanted.
- Proposal E (not run): lyx extracts the target's citations (paths, backticked symbols) as the manifest's starting list without loading code, leaving the choice of what to read to the master; 22 of the 25 files the original forks needed are cited in the target, the other 3 one hop away.

entries.title: Weaver: a cold-start implementer beside Webster, with model escalation
entries.brief: A second implementer built on Millhouse Builder: a fresh agent per batch with its own model, escalating the model when an agent fails; Webster stays fork-based
entries.body:
## Idea (operator, 2026-10-11)

Webster stays fork-based: its implementer and verify-fix forks start at once with Master's context and run on Master's model.
Weaver is a second implementer beside it, built on Millhouse's "Builder" (skill `mill-go`), that runs a cold-start agent per batch, so each agent can take its own model, and escalates the model when an agent fails.

## Seen (research, 2026-10-11)

- Webster spawns one cold agent today: the recovery strand.
  When a fork reports `stuck` or writes no report twice, Master runs `lyx webster recover-batch` (`contracts/stencils/webster/webster-template-master.md`), which starts a fresh shuttle/reed strand with a full cold-start prompt (`internal/websterengine/recoverbatch.go`).
  Its model is `webster.yaml` `recovery` (default `opus[high]`), against `master` at `sonnet[medium]`; that is Webster's only model escalation, and a batch gets at most two recoveries.
- Builder (`plugins/mill/skills/mill-go-base/SKILL.md` in the Millhouse worktree) is a lean orchestrator that never reads cards or diffs.
  Per batch it starts a fresh, non-fork agent with a model from config (`roles.implementer.model`), and the agent reads only its batch file and the overview's Shared Decisions.
  It has no automatic model escalation: a stuck batch gets one fresh retry on the same tier, then a plan edit with a `## Prior failure` note, then a question to the parent.
- Millhouse's cold starts were slow: each agent read much background and loaded its tools before it began work.
  Likely further costs visible in the skill: a review loop per batch, finalize replaying every batch's verify in turn, and a state commit on every status change.

## Shape

Weaver is, in effect, Webster's recovery strand used as the normal path.

- From Webster: the Go bracket verbs (begin-batch, record-batch, recover-batch), the report contract and classification, suspect paths, partition and sequencing, the plan-level verify gate and failure ladder, the shuttle/reed spawn path, and `RenderRecoveryPrompt` with `uncommitted_paths` and the failure digest.
- From Builder: a cold, scoped agent per batch that reads only its cards and Shared Decisions, a model and effort per role per spawn, and a one-shot self-resolve before halting.
- New in neither: an escalation ladder per failed attempt, for example `sonnet` → `opus` → `opus[high]`, set in config.
- Open: how to keep cold-start cost down (a kick-start pack per batch, see `kick-start-pack`), and how a run chooses Weaver over Webster (recipe row or config).

entries.title: Startup probe sleeps 10 s between checks; batten window waits for it
entries.brief: awaitStartup checks the pane every 10 s, so every shuttle start and every batten window waits about 10 s after the agent is up
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-11)

`lyx batten run <slug> --window` opens the Konsole window about 11 s after the child loom run is spawned, every time (per-role-models 11.2 s; gate-test-hygiene, small-fixes-batch, seats-chair-first 11.0–11.1 s).
The Claude driver is up within about a second; the rest is a fixed wait.

- Batten opens the window only after `lyx loom start --no-attach` exits (`internal/battenshed/innerrun.go`, `innerRunProducer.Call`; `internal/battencli/wire.go`, `Spawn` runs it with `cmd.Run()`).
- `loom start` returns only after shuttle's `start` (`internal/shuttleengine/run.go`) has passed `awaitStartup` (`internal/shuttleengine/wait.go`), which captures the pane and between checks sleeps `poll_interval_ms × liveness_every_n_polls`, 1000 ms × 10 = 10 s.
  The 10 s cadence is deliberate there, to avoid stray keypresses during trust-prompt dismissal.
- The same `awaitStartup` gates every shuttle start, so every agent a run spawns (reviewers, fixers, judges, seeds, Webster's Master) likely waits up to 10 s longer than it needs to.
- Seats (bench pair `dbench-ohsh`, 2026-10-11): the chair went live at 10:44:16 and the advisor at 10:44:32, 16 s later, since the advisors start only after the chair; the chair's own `awaitStartup` wait likely accounts for most of it, and each advisor start adds its own. Not yet traced.
- The window runs only `lyx reed attach` in the pair (`internal/termwindow/termwindow.go`), which needs the pair's tmux session, up about 0.1 s after the spawn.

## Idea, ranked by gain

1. Probe every `poll_interval_ms` (1 s) during startup and replay the trust-prompt dismissal at most once per 10 s; saves about 8–9 s on every shuttle start, not only batten.
2. Open the window as soon as the pair's reed session exists rather than after `loom start` exits; saves about 11 s on each batten start, and batten then has to handle a spawn that fails after the window is open.
3. Minor, under 2 s: Seed-Child's `main-weft` push after the spawn, and no segment-color typing before the window opens.

entries.title: Parent-review wait lets the idle writer cache expire before a reject
entries.brief: A reject after more than 5 minutes resumes the writer or chair on a cold cache; keep it warm with a periodic ping, or resume a fresh session
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-11)

While Discussion-Write's parent-review gate waits, the writer or seats chair and its advisors stay alive and idle (`internal/shuttleengine/wait.go:284-299`, `372-383`; advisors kept by `KeepPane: !isChair`, `internal/seatengine/prompt.go:161`, stopped only in `join`, `internal/seatengine/engine.go:245-252`).

- On approve nobody takes another turn: the writer's strand is removed without a message (`wait.go:385-389`) and advisors are killed (`engine.go:251`), so the cache does not matter.
- On reject the findings are typed into the same idle session (`wait.go:391-399`, `internal/parentreview/gate.go:165-170`).
  If the review took more than the 5-minute prompt-cache lifetime, that turn re-reads the whole writer context uncached, which is the expensive case.
- While delivery is unrecorded, the gate re-sends the delivery prompt up to three times at least a minute apart (`gate.go:20-22`, `190`); each re-send is a writer turn that may land on a cold cache.

## Idea

Keep the waiting writer's cache warm, the way the Burler fixer already does: `lyx burler await` caps each wait below the 5-minute lifetime so every re-run keeps the fixer's cache warm (`internal/burlercli/await.go:25`).
The operator suggests a ping injected into the idle writer about every 4 minutes while the gate waits.

- A ping is a small cached turn; it pays off only when a reject is likely, so weigh its cost against the cold re-read on reject.
- Alternative: on a reject that arrives after the cache has expired, start a fresh session with only the decision record, the support log and the findings instead of resuming the old context.
- Advisors need no ping: they never take another turn after the chair's record exists.

entries.title: TwillDiscusser: a Discussion writer that forks lens reviewers before it writes
entries.brief: Single-LLM Discussion-Write producer: explore, fork waiting lens forks, write, forks review the record as outsiders; forks keep their cache warm themselves
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-11)

The first Discussion bench (`docs/research/discussion-bench.md`, 7d439cf71) found that no seats chair with an advisor wrote a better draft than the same chair alone, and that an Opus or high-effort Sonnet advisor roughly doubled the cost.
Each seats advisor is a standalone session at full price that re-reads the code itself; the operator names this as part of the problem.
Each configuration ran once on one task, so the noise is unmeasured.

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-11)

`TwillDiscusser`: a new Discussion-Write producer, chosen with `discussion_producer: twill` beside `single` and `seats`, that brings Burler's lens fan into the writer's own session.
To shed it is a single-LLM producer; the forks live inside the writer's Claude Code session, so the new parts are its stencil, the lens texts and a wait command, not the shed engine.

1. The writer, on a strong model such as `opus[medium]`, explores the task and code in full on its own.
2. Ready to write, it does not write yet: it forks itself once per lens.
3. Each fork is told to wait until the decision record exists, and does no lens work before then.
4. The writer, which is not a fork, writes the whole decision record and support log.
5. Each fork then reviews the written record through its lens and returns its findings to the writer.
6. The writer takes in the findings and finalises the record.

Gains:

- Every fork runs on the writer's strong model.
- Every fork inherits the writer's exploration, so it reads that prefix from cache rather than re-reading the code.
- The forks did not write the record, so they read it as outsiders rather than defending decisions they made; forks spawned after the draft would carry its writing in their context and tend to polish it rather than question it.
- No seats engine or SendMessage rounds.

Lenses: each fork gets a focus, as Burler's lens forks do (for example correctness, error handling, test gaps, scope, consistency with the board); Burler's fan lens texts are the starting point.

## Cache while the forks wait

Writing the record often takes longer than the 5-minute prompt-cache lifetime, so a fork that waits idle would re-read its whole context uncached when it wakes, losing the cache gain.
Nothing outside can inject a ping into a fork, so each fork keeps its own cache warm the way the Burler fixer does with `lyx burler await` (`internal/burlercli/await.go:25`):

- the fork runs a foreground wait for the record file, capped at about 4 minutes;
- if the cap is reached first, the fork takes one short turn that only re-runs the wait, which reads its context from cache and resets the 5-minute clock;
- when the record appears, the wait returns at once and the lens review starts.

This needs a general wait command (wait for a file, with a cap), since `lyx burler await` is built for the fixer; the same command serves the writer waiting on parent review (`parent-review-cold-cache`).

## Scope of this task

Build the `twill` producer, its stencil and lens texts, the general capped wait command, the config wiring and the docs.
The bench below runs after landing, from the prime, as its own job.

## Later: Plan

The same pattern fits the Plan writer, whose review findings are often enumerable (a test missing from a card's `Edit:` list, fixtures not enumerated) and whose exploration is larger, so forks save more; it comes after `TwillDiscusser` has been benched (operator, 2026-10-11).
Keep the fork-wait-review stencil part and the wait command reusable for that.

## Bench

Compare, three runs each on the same reference task, so the spread is measured too:

- `opus[medium]` with `TwillDiscusser`;
- `opus[medium]` alone;
- `opus[high]` alone, the first bench's best draft.

Measure wall time, price per configuration, the draft against the reference final discussion judged on the merits, and where possible how many Discussion-Review rounds each draft needs.
The open question whether Burler's fan findings are worth their cost applies here too.

entries.title: Plan gaps: inserting a card, unreachable prescribed refusals
entries.brief: Give the fixer a sanctioned way to insert or remove a card, and make plan review check that every prescribed refusal is reachable
entries.body:
Two gaps in how plans are written and reviewed, merged into one task (operator, 2026-10-11).

## Inserting or removing a card (was `plan-card-insert`, issue #508)

Plan cards are numbered contiguously and each card file name is tied to its number.
A Plan-Review fix that needed one new card ahead of card 8 therefore renumbered cards 8 to 19, twelve files.

The fixer rules allow file changes only through Edit or Write and name no way to rename or remove a file.
The fixer rewrote each card under its new name and removed the old files with `rm`, which the rules neither allow nor forbid.

This is abnormal: a routine plan edit forces a fixer to guess at an unstated rule and do a bulk, error-prone rewrite.

What to do, either of:

- add a plan verb that inserts a card and renumbers the rest;
- state a rule for removing a file inside the fixer's write surface.

Provenance: task `driver-context`; note `burler-plan-r1.md`.

## Unreachable prescribed refusals (was `plan-refusal-reachability`, issue #516)

A plan card prescribed a refusal branch (a zero-batch refusal after an accepted auto-rebaseline) with a fixed signature.
Review of the implementation flagged that no test reaches the refusal; the fixing agent then found that no plan can reach it, because the plan parser refuses a cardless plan before `Run` forms any batch.
The branch was kept and its text pinned with a golden test of the error constructor, which conflicts with the rule against code for impossible states.

This is abnormal because the plan passed its Plan-Bouncer and Plan-Burler rounds with a prescribed refusal that is unreachable by construction, and the contradiction surfaced only after the code was written.

What to do: have plan review (or the plan-time checks) verify that every refusal a card prescribes is reachable from some input that passes upstream validation, or require the card to say how a test reaches it.

Provenance: task `webster-replan-state`, from note `burler-webster-r1.md`.

entries.title: Pane injection never merges with the operator draft, and batten survives a draft
entries.brief: Defer and atomically send injected text, guard the Enter, and keep batten alive through a busy driver pane so teardown still runs.
entries.body:
Two faults around lyx typing into a Claude pane, merged into one task (operator, 2026-10-11).

## Injected text merges with the operator's draft (was `pane-inject-race`)

### Seen (2026-10-11, operator)

Text lyx injects into a Claude pane (batten notices, resume pointers, driver resume lines, `/clear`, `/compact`, `/reload-plugins`) regularly merges with what the operator is typing, or wipes it.
The draft guard checks the input box once, before typing, and the send then spends about a second typing into the pane (Escape, 300 ms sleep, text, settle reads, Enter) with nothing stopping the operator from typing in between.
The first Enter of a verified send (`confirmSubmitted`, `internal/shuttleengine/send.go:346`) is never checked against the box, so a merged draft is submitted.
`boxHoldsSentText` (`internal/shuttleengine/run.go`) only matches the leading 48 characters, so a merged box reads as "holds the sent text" and gets further Enters.
`ClearSession`, `CompactSession` and `ReloadPlugins` (`internal/shuttleengine/session.go`) type the command and a blind Enter on the strength of the caller's earlier probe, so `/clear` can land on an operator draft.
`judgeReadiness` (`internal/shuttleengine/readiness.go:83`) reads ready when no box is found, so a menu or picker on screen passes the guard, and the leading Escape then closes it.
The leading Escape can complete a double-Esc that clears the operator's draft, or interrupt a turn the operator just started.

### Wanted

A check that refuses the Enter after the text merged comes too late: the operator's draft is already spoiled.
So prevent the merge first, and keep the Enter check only as a last guard (operator, 2026-10-11):

1. **Defer while the operator types.** Hold an injection while the attached client's `#{client_activity}` is under a few seconds old and the target pane is its active pane; the injection waits in a queue and is retried, never dropped.
2. **Send text and Enter atomically.** `load-buffer` + `paste-buffer -p -d` + `send-keys Enter` as one tmux command list, and drop the leading Escape and the 300 ms settle, so the window between check and submit shrinks from about a second to the capture-to-write gap.
   Needs a live check that Claude Code treats a paste-end followed by Enter as a submit.
3. **Last guard: check the box right before Enter.** Press Enter only when the box holds exactly the sent text (or the paste placeholder).
   On a mismatch, send no Enter, never clear or edit the box, and requeue the injection until the box reads empty again (the operator sent or cleared the draft).
4. Route `/clear`, `/compact`, `/reload-plugins`, color and session-rename through the same path, and treat an unreadable box as not idle in `judgeReadiness`.

Later, not in this task: file-based notice delivery to the orch through a Stop hook, so fewer notices are typed at all.

## A draft in the driver pane kills batten, and the pair is never torn down (was `batten-draft-teardown`)

### Seen (2026-10-11, gate-test-hygiene, PR #537)

After `lyx loom approve` at PR-Gate, batten's Run-Shed tried to resume the parked driver and failed with `shuttle: the session is not idle ... the input box holds a draft: "Tok"`.
`internal/battenshed/innerrun.go:816` treats any resume error other than `ErrChildNotParked` as fatal, so batten went `failed` and exited.
The orch then drove the loom run to done by hand with `lyx loom start`.
Nobody resumed batten, so Worktree-Teardown never ran: the pair, its empty reed session and its weft branch stayed, and no `archive/<slug>/<tip>` tag was pushed.
`lyx batten run <slug>` afterwards closes it: Run-Shed sees the done child and moves on to Worktree-Teardown.

### Wanted

- A "session not idle / draft" resume error is not fatal: batten retries it the way `ErrChildNotParked` is retried (with the queue above, the resume waits for the box to clear), or halts `blocked` with the remedy "clear the draft, then `lyx batten run <slug>`".
- A batten run that is `failed` while its child loom run is `done` is flagged, naming `lyx batten run <slug>` as the step that closes it.
- The orch's after-landing routine checks that `lyx batten status <slug>` is done, and otherwise runs `lyx batten run <slug>`.

entries.title: Rename the darn writer row to Darn-Write
entries.brief: The recipe and its writer row are both named darn; rename the row to Darn-Write like loom's -Write rows.
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-11)

`darn` names both the recipe and its writer row `Darn` (engine `DarnWrite`), which is confusing.
The loom recipe avoids this: its rows are named for what they do (`Discussion-Write`, `Plan-Write`, `Webster`), and no row is named `Loom`.

## Wanted

Rename the darn writer row from `Darn` to `Darn-Write`, matching the loom `-Write` rows and the engine name `DarnWrite`.
Row names are durable on-disk identities pinned against `internal/loomshed` `Name*` constants, so rename the constant with the row, and keep an in-flight darn run whose status names the old row resumable.
Update every reference: recipe edges (`PR-Gate`'s `on_stuck`, the perch rows `darn-perch` added), docs, stencils and tests.
